newsitem.title: UK: Eurolira trade booms as fast-moving Italy attracts.
newsitem.headline: Eurolira trade booms as fast-moving Italy attracts.

text.p: For traders on LIFFE, the Eurolira futures pit is the place to be these days.
Eurolira futures volume in London is booming as investors revel in a mix of a stable economy and aspirations for a single European currency, seasoned with a pinch of political wrangling.

While the investment community has historically been wary of markets in Italy -- a country which is on its 55th government since World War Two -- trade in Italian derivatives has always been popular for its hedging and speculative possibilities.
Added to that, Italy's progress toward European monetary union has brought in a new era of respectability, traders said.

"We've seen a progression in the way investors view Italian markets," said Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at Co-operative Bank in London. "The volatility is now at manageable levels. It gives investors interesting opportunities, rather than just the headaches it used to give."

Volume of Eurolira futures traded on LIFFE, the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange, has risen sharply, with more than one million contracts traded last month, compared with just over 400,000 in March 1996.
In the first three months of this year, 3.3 million contracts traded, 153 percent more than the year-ago period.
Traders said it was noteworthy the progress made in reforming the Italian pension system has been enough to eclipse such issues as the latest political upset over Albania.
"Interest is much wider, and new investors are coming into Italian markets because of their underlying confidence in the country," said Simon Lamb, a broker at UBS on the LIFFE floor.
"There is increasing evidence of interest in hedging lira flows using Eurolira futures, and also of speculators trading it as a commodity," he said.

Beauchamp said investors had switched their focus from more mature derivatives markets such as gilt options, which offered fewer chances to make -- or lose -- money because they trade in a more muted way.
Lamb agreed, "If you want volatility, then Italian assets provide it. That has spurred both BTP Italian bonds) and Eurolira volumes."
Beauchamp said Eurolira futures were seeing extra trade amid expectations of an Italian interest rate cut, and were also boosted by the lira.

A Eurolira futures trader at a British bank on LIFFE said there were days when activity in the front month contracts was greater in Eurolira than in Euromarks, the benchmark European interest rate contract.
He said there was speculation on the floor the Eurolira pit would need to be physically enlarged to take account of the greater trade.
"It can get pretty crammed in here," he said, leaning out of a packed pit of brightly jacketed dealers.

LIFFE operating officer Karin Forseke said on Friday there could be a slight expansion of the Eurolira pit in June, but pressures of space on the floor meant it was unlikely to be of any significant size.

"We have great shortage of space and a huge reconfiguration in progress which we know is causing discomfort," she said. "We have just expanded the Euromark pit and primarily new space will be given to the mark products."
